The knapsack family

Recap · 10 minutes
The 0/1 knapsack in one array
1
State
dp[c] is the best value with capacity at most c, using the items processed so far.
2
Transition
Skip item i, or take it on top of dp[c − w]: dp[c] = max(dp[c], dp[c − w] + v).
3
Direction
Loop c from W down to w, so dp[c − w] still excludes item i.
Demo 1 · Watch the loop
Descending or ascending?
C++ implementation
0/1 knapsack, one array
// dp[c] = best total value with capacity at most c, using the items processed so far long long dp[W + 1] = {};                 // all zeros: with no items, every capacity gives value 0 for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {            // handle the items one by one     // Go from big c DOWN to w[i]. Then dp[c - w[i]] has not been updated for item i yet,     // so it still describes "without item i", and item i is used at most once.     for (int c = W; c >= w[i]; c--) {         // either keep the old dp[c] (skip item i) or put item i into a bag of capacity c - w[i]         dp[c] = max(dp[c], dp[c - w[i]] + v[i]);     } } cout << dp[W];                            // best value with capacity at most W // Time O(n * W), memory O(W)
C++ implementation
0/1 knapsack, listing the chosen items
// dp[i][c] = best value using only the first i items with capacity c (a full table, O(n * W) memory) // take[i][c] = true if the best choice for (i, c) takes item i for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {     for (int c = 0; c <= W; c++) {         dp[i][c] = dp[i-1][c];                               // option 1: skip item i         if (c >= w[i] && dp[i-1][c - w[i]] + v[i] > dp[i][c]) {             dp[i][c] = dp[i-1][c - w[i]] + v[i];             // option 2: take item i, it is better             take[i][c] = true;                               // remember the decision         }     } } // Walk back from (n, W): if item i was taken, record it and use up its weight for (int i = n, c = W; i >= 1; i--)     if (take[i][c]) { chosen.push_back(i); c -= w[i]; }
C++ implementation
Unbounded knapsack: each item any number of times
// dp[c] = best total value with capacity at most c, with an unlimited supply of every item long long dp[W + 1] = {};                 // all zeros for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {     // Go UP this time. dp[c - w[i]] may already contain item i, so item i can be taken again     // and again: that is exactly what "unlimited copies" means.     for (int c = w[i]; c <= W; c++) {         dp[c] = max(dp[c], dp[c - w[i]] + v[i]);     } } cout << dp[W]; // The code is identical to the 0/1 version: only the direction of the c loop changed. // Counting the number of ways to make change uses the same upward loop with // ways[c] += ways[c - w[i]] (start with ways[0] = 1).
Demo 2 · Watch the pieces
Bounded knapsack by binary splitting
C++ implementation
Bounded knapsack: at most k copies of each item
// Item i has weight w[i], value v[i] and may be taken at most k[i] times. // Idea: split k[i] into pieces of size 1, 2, 4, ... plus a remainder. Every count from 0 to k[i] // is a sum of distinct pieces, so each piece can be treated as one ordinary 0/1 item. vector<int> pw, pv;                              // weights and values of the new 0/1 items for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {     int left = k[i];     for (int p = 1; left > 0; p <<= 1) {         int cnt = min(p, left);                  // piece size: 1, 2, 4, ..., then whatever is left         pw.push_back(cnt * w[i]);                // a piece of cnt copies weighs cnt * w[i]         pv.push_back(cnt * v[i]);                // and is worth cnt * v[i]         left -= cnt;     } } // Now run the 0/1 knapsack (descending loop) over the items pw[], pv[]. // Number of items: sum of log(k[i]), so the time is O(W * sum of log k[i]).
Exact capacity
Must the bag be completely full?
At most W
All dp[c] start at 0. Unused capacity is allowed, so dp[c] is the best value that fits in c.
fill(dp, dp + W + 1, 0);
Exactly W
Only dp[0] = 0 is reachable at the start. Everything else is −INF until some items fill that capacity.
fill(dp, dp + W + 1, -INF); dp[0] = 0;

C++ implementation
Subset sum, with bitsets
// Subset sum: can some subset of a[1..n] add up to exactly S? // Plain version: ok[c] is true if the sum c can be made. Descending loop: each number is used once. bool ok[S + 1] = {}; ok[0] = true;                                  // the empty subset makes 0 for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++)     for (int c = S; c >= a[i]; c--)         ok[c] = ok[c] || ok[c - a[i]];         // reach c by adding a[i] to a reachable c - a[i] // Bitset version: bit c says whether the sum c is reachable. // Shifting left by a[i] moves every reachable sum c to c + a[i], all at once. bitset<100001> reach; reach[0] = 1; for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) reach |= reach << a[i];   // about 64 times faster cout << reach[S];                              // time O(n * S / 64)
C++ implementation
Huge capacity, small values
// Use this when W is huge (up to 10^9) but the total value V = v[1] + ... + v[n] is small (say 10^5). // dp[x] = the MINIMUM total weight needed to collect value exactly x. long long dp[V + 1]; fill(dp, dp + V + 1, INF);                     // INF means "this value cannot be reached" dp[0] = 0;                                     // value 0 costs nothing for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++)     for (int x = V; x >= v[i]; x--)            // descending: each item at most once         dp[x] = min(dp[x], dp[x - v[i]] + w[i]); // The answer is the largest value x whose minimum weight still fits into the bag. int best = 0; for (int x = 0; x <= V; x++)     if (dp[x] <= W) best = x; cout << best;                                  // time O(n * V), memory O(V)
Pitfalls
Three classic knapsack bugs
01
Wrong direction
Descending for 0/1, ascending for unbounded. Mixing them silently changes the problem.
02
Wrong initial values
At most W starts at 0, exactly W starts at −INF. Watch overflow when adding to ±INF.
03
Size and type
n × W must fit time and memory. Values need long long. Huge W: dp over value.

Session 2
LIS and LCS
Longest increasing subsequence · Longest common subsequence
LIS · 20 minutes
Longest increasing subsequence
Problem
A sequence a of n numbers. Find the longest subsequence with strictly increasing values. Elements need not be adjacent.
Example: 5 2 8 6 3 6 9 7 has the LIS 2 3 6 9, length 4.
State
dp[i] is the length of the longest increasing subsequence that ends exactly at index i. Think about its previous element j.
dp[i] = 1 + max( dp[j] ) over j < i with a[j] < a[i]
If no such j exists, dp[i] = 1. The answer is the maximum of all dp[i].
Demo 3 · Watch the table fill
LIS in O(n²)
C++ implementation
LIS in O(n²), with the sequence
// dp[i] = length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence that ENDS at index i // par[i] = index of the previous element in that subsequence (-1 if it starts at i) for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {     dp[i] = 1; par[i] = -1;                    // a single element is an increasing sequence     for (int j = 0; j < i; j++)                // try every earlier element as the predecessor         if (a[j] < a[i] && dp[j] + 1 > dp[i]) {             dp[i] = dp[j] + 1;                 // extend the best subsequence ending at j             par[i] = j;                        // remember where we came from         } } int end = max_element(dp, dp + n) - dp;        // the LIS ends where dp is largest for (int i = end; i != -1; i = par[i])         // follow the par[] links backwards     seq.push_back(a[i]); reverse(seq.begin(), seq.end());               // collected from the end, so reverse it
Faster LIS
Keep the smallest possible endings
1
The tails array
tails[k] is the smallest possible last value of an increasing subsequence of length k + 1.
2
Always sorted
A longer subsequence cannot end with a smaller value than a shorter one can.
3
Binary search
For each value find the first tail that is at least as large and replace it, or append.
A smaller ending is never worse: anything that can follow a large ending can also follow a small one.
Demo 4 · Watch the tails
LIS in O(n log n)
C++ implementation
LIS in O(n log n)
// tails[k] = smallest possible LAST value of an increasing subsequence of length k + 1. // tails is always sorted, so binary search can tell where each new value belongs. vector<int> tails; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {     // first position whose value is >= a[i] (for NON-decreasing sequences use upper_bound)     int pos = lower_bound(tails.begin(), tails.end(), a[i]) - tails.begin();     if (pos == (int)tails.size())         tails.push_back(a[i]);                 // a[i] is bigger than every tail: the LIS grows     else         tails[pos] = a[i];                     // a[i] is a smaller ending for length pos + 1 } cout << tails.size();                          // the LIS length, in O(n log n) // Note: tails is NOT the LIS itself, only its size is the answer. // To print the LIS also store, for every i, the index of the element that ended at pos - 1 // when a[i] was placed, then follow those links backwards from the last tail.
LCS · 17 minutes
Longest common subsequence
Problem
Two strings s and t. Find the longest string that is a subsequence of both.
Example: AGCAT and GAC share AC, length 2.
State
dp[i][j] is the LCS length of the first i letters of s and the first j letters of t.
dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1 if s[i-1] == t[j-1]
dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]) otherwise
Demo 5 · Watch the table fill
LCS of AGCAT and GAC
C++ implementation
LCS length
// dp[i][j] = length of the LCS of the first i characters of s and the first j characters of t // Row 0 and column 0 stay 0: an empty prefix has nothing in common with anything. int n = s.size(), m = t.size(); for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {     for (int j = 1; j <= m; j++) {         if (s[i-1] == t[j-1])                  // strings are 0-based, the table is 1-based             dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1;       // equal last characters: extend the diagonal         else             dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j],         // drop the last character of s ...                            dp[i][j-1]);        // ... or the last character of t, keep the better     } } cout << dp[n][m];                              // LCS length of the two whole strings // Time O(n * m). Memory O(n * m), or O(m) if only the length is needed (keep two rows).
C++ implementation
LCS: rebuilding the string
// Walk back from dp[n][m] and rebuild one LCS (the letters come out in reverse order) string lcs; int i = n, j = m; while (i > 0 && j > 0) {     if (s[i-1] == t[j-1]) {                    // this character belongs to the LCS         lcs += s[i-1];         i--; j--;                              // continue diagonally     } else if (dp[i-1][j] >= dp[i][j-1]) {         i--;                                   // the value came from above: skip s[i-1]     } else {         j--;                                   // the value came from the left: skip t[j-1]     } } reverse(lcs.begin(), lcs.end());               // we collected it from the end, so reverse cout << lcs;
Cousins of LCS
Same table, other questions
Edit distance
Fewest insertions, deletions and replacements to turn s into t. Same table, min of three neighbours.
Shortest common supersequence
Its length is n + m − LCS(s, t).
Longest palindromic subsequence
Equals LCS(s, reverse of s).
LIS through LCS
For distinct values, LIS(a) = LCS(a, sorted a). Slower, but a useful view.

Pitfalls
Three classic LIS and LCS bugs
01
Strict or not
lower_bound gives strictly increasing, upper_bound gives non-decreasing.
02
Index shift
The table is 1-based, the strings are 0-based: dp[i][j] uses s[i-1], t[j-1].
03
Lost path
Two-row memory or the tails array cannot print the sequence. Store parents or the table.
